column2: If the mother has died while the father lives and the paternal grandmother is still living, the sapindana should be performed together with the grandmother.
Truly, truly, and again truly, hear my word: for men who have died on earth and whose rice-ball has not been joined with the ancestors,
whatever their sons give in many ways does not reach them — neither the hantakara offering in their name, nor the shraddha, nor the handful of water.
After the panchaka period everything for him should be done; otherwise distress arises for his sons and kinsmen.
One who dies under these constellations brings loss to his house; or, if he dies within the constellation period, his cremation is still prescribed,
for men's cremation is performed at once, for the sake of the immediate offering. Cremation at a tirtha, bringing immediate oblation, is meritorious and best.
It must be performed duly by brahmins, with mantras and according to rule. Then effigies are placed beside the corpse —
four made of darbha grass, consecrated with mantras by brahmins; then the cremation should be performed together with those effigies.
Then, at the end of the period of impurity, the son should perform the excellent pacificatory rite.
A man who dies during the panchaka does not attain a good destiny; for him one should give sesame, cows, gold and ghee.
The gift given to brahmins destroys all misfortune; and at the end of the impurity, through his good sons, that departed one attains his goal.
A vessel, sandals, an umbrella, a gold coin and a pair of garments are given as the fee, O brahmin, releasing him from all sins.
For children, the old and the sick who die in the panchaka, whoever does not perform the prescribed rite meets with obstacles.
In the shraddha for the departed eighteen things should be avoided: blessings, doubled darbha grass, the pranava, and the single rice-ball,
the offering into fire, the leftovers, the shraddha to the Vishvedevas, the scattered offering, the cry of svadha; and one should not utter the word 'ancestors.'
One should not use the word 'anu,' nor the invocation, nor the firebrand; one should not go to the boundary, nor perform the circumambulation and dismissal.
The brahmin should not perform the sesame oblation or the final full oblation; if he performs the Vaishvadeva, the performer goes to a low state.
The first set of sixteen is known as the 'unclean shraddhas': at the place of death, at the door, halfway along the road, at the pyre, in the hand of the corpse,

the fifth for the beings dwelling in the cremation ground, for neighbours; the sixth is declared at the gathering of the bones; and the ten rice-balls of the ten days — this is proclaimed the first set of sixteen shraddhas.
Now hear from me, Tarkshya, the second, middle set of sixteen: here eleven shraddhas are to be performed according to rule,
those to Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva and the rest, and another set of five shraddhas; thus those who know the truth speak of this set of sixteen.
The twelve monthly shraddhas, the shraddha on the eleventh day, the one arising at three fortnights, and two for the gaps — these, O bird, make sixteen.
Having performed the first for the purification of the corpse and the other three sets of sixteen, one should join him with the fifty for the purification of the ancestral line.
One who is joined without the fifty does not share in the line. The forty-eight shraddhas destroy the state of a ghost;
with forty-nine one comes near the line, and truly he is to be joined by the fiftieth shraddha as the link.
(Now the rite for the corpse.) On the bier the hands and feet of the corpse should be bound; if this rule is not followed, it is overpowered by pishachas.
If the corpse is carried out at night the realm is free of fear. The corpse should not be let go; if it is let go, an evil touch brings a bad destiny.
Betel, tooth-sticks, eating and marital relations should be avoided, and the offering of rice-balls, while a corpse lies in the village.
If anyone knowingly eats as he pleases while a corpse lies in the village, that food is to be regarded as flesh and that water as blood.
Bathing, giving, japa, oblation, libations and worship of the gods, while a corpse lies in the village, are for purification according to the duty of kinsmen.
Such is the conduct of kinsmen and relatives, O lord of birds; one who neglects the duty of kinsmen is stained by the sin of the departed.
Sin committed at home is purified by bathing at a tirtha; but sin committed at a tirtha becomes as fixed as if bonded with adamant,
and one suffers for it, without doubt, as long as the moon, sun and stars endure. Gifts given there become imperishable.
When someone is gravely ill, even poor men should give — cows, sesame, gold, and especially the seven grains.
Seeing a generous man, all the dwellers of heaven rejoice, together with the sages, Dharma and Chitragupta, always.
As long as wealth is in one's own control, one should give it to brahmins; after death all is in others' hands — who will give it out of kindness?
Whatever wealth sons place in a brahmin's hand in their father's name, by that they make themselves wealthy, with sons and great-grandsons.
A gift for the father is said to be a hundredfold, for the mother a thousandfold, for a sister a hundred thousandfold, and for a brother imperishable.
If they do not give, out of greed, heedlessness or delusion, then after death they all grieve, 'We were misers and sinners.'
For wealth gained with great hardship and fickle by nature there is only one proper course, giving; all others lead to misfortune.
Death laughs at the one who guards his body, and the earth at the one who hoards wealth, like an unchaste wife at a husband who dotes on his son.
The righteous, gentle man remains detached even on gaining great wealth; he regards himself and his wealth as grass, Tarkshya.
For him there are no calamities, no net of delusion, and at the time of death no fear arising from Yama's messengers.
Seven thousand years for death in water, eleven in fire, sixteen in wind; sixty in great battle, eighty for dying at a cowshed; and for death by fasting, O Kashyapa, an imperishable goal.
From the eleventh day onward a pot called drdha, filled with cooked food and water, should be given daily for a full year.
Large water vessels and pitchers should be given; one of them is the vardhani, and in it a vessel of bamboo.
One should cover them with cloth, worship them with fragrant substances, and especially have them given, filled with water, to brahmins.
Day after day, making the resolve according to rule, O lord of birds, it should be given to a brahmin of good family, endowed with Vedic conduct,
possessed of learning and good conduct — never to a fool. One rich in Vedic conduct is able both to cross over and to carry others across.
One who builds even a leaf hut that keeps off cold, wind and heat and gives it to a learned brahmin with a family
is honoured in heaven for three and a half crores of years.
A pure woman of the same class who follows her dead husband attains heaven after death for as many years as there are hairs on her body.
She who leaves sons, grandsons and the rest and follows her husband — both of them attain heaven, adorned by celestial women.
Even if she has committed many sins and always intended to wrong her husband, she who follows her husband washes them all away.
Even if the husband is a wrongdoer who has committed great sins, the woman devoted to him removes all his sin.
One who regularly gives even a mouthful of food every day goes in a celestial car fitted with four fly-whisks.
Whatever sin a man has committed up to the end of his life, all of it is destroyed by giving a year's livelihood.
Sin of past, present and future, accumulated over three births, is all washed away by arranging the marriage of a brahmin's daughter.
A step-well equals ten wells, a lake equals ten step-wells, and a water-shed in a waterless forest equals ten lakes.
A step-well in a waterless land, a gift to a poor brahmin — one who shows compassion to living beings becomes a lord of heaven.
By these and other good deeds one shares in heaven; obtaining all that fruit, he attains the highest standing.
Giving up trivial pursuits, one should always be righteous; giving, self-control and compassion — these three are the essence on earth.
A gift to a poor good man, worship of an abandoned linga, and the funeral rites of a helpless dead person give the fruit of a crore of sacrifices.
With an earthen vessel and water mixed with sesame, and finally with earth, a man becomes pure by bathing.
He should give a gift to the assembly, and gold and a cow and bull to a brahmin; a kshatriya should give double, and a vaishya triple;
a shudra should give four times as much wealth to a brahmin. In this order the four classes are purified.
For a child dying in the seventh or eighth year before the domestic sacraments, the period of impurity is reckoned in days according to the number of years.
For those who die for the sake of brahmins, for women, in cattle raids, or in battle, impurity lasts one night.
No ill befalls brahmins in auspicious rites, nor the best of men who perform the last rites of a helpless dead person;
no ill befalls those who assist a brahmin; for them purification is declared to be immediate, by plunging into water.
When shudras have finished and come to the water's edge, they should then be looked upon by a brahmin — so say the knowers of the Veda.
One should place a hundred on the two thighs and thirty on the two shanks, four at the penis and six at the two testicles, and ten at the toes; thus should the bones be arranged.
One should place a coconut in place of the head, a gourd at the palate, the five jewels in the mouth, and a banana on the tongue.
For the intestines a lotus stalk, for the breath a baluka plant, for the marrow meda, and cow's urine for the urine;
sulphur for the bodily elements, orpiment and red arsenic; mercury in place of semen and brass for the feces;
red arsenic on the limbs, sesame paste at the joints, barley flour for the flesh, and honey;
banyan roots for the hair, deerskin for the skin, palm leaves for the ears, and gunja berries for the breasts;
a hundred-petalled lotus for the nose, a lotus at the navel, brinjals for the testicles, and a fine carrot for the penis.
Ghee is to be placed at the navel and tin at the loincloth; pearls on the breasts, and the head anointed with saffron;
with camphor, aloe-wood incense and fine fragrant garlands; the garment should be of silk thread, and gold placed on the heart.
Riddhi and Vriddhi for the two arms, cowries for the eyes, vermilion at the corners of the eyes, with offerings of betel and the like.

Having furnished the effigy of the departed with all herbs, one should perform the worship as prescribed; and for one who kept the sacred fire, one should place the sacrificial vessels in order according to rule.
With the verse 'Shirome shrih' and 'Punantu Varuna,' having purified the departed with water from rice, sal and stone,
one should give a gentle milch cow in the name of Vishnu.
Sesame, iron, gold, cotton, salt, the seven grains, land and cows — each one is declared a gift; then one should give the vessel of sesame and the gift of sandals.
The great gifts should be given, and the vessel of sesame; then the Vaitarani cow should be given, adorned with all ornaments.
The self-controlled one should perform the Vaishnava shraddha for the release of the departed; then he should perform the release of the departed, contemplating Vishnu in his heart,
remembering 'Om Vishnu' and the departed and his death; then he should perform the cremation, and the impurity lasts three days.
The one who performs the ten-day rites should offer rice-balls for the nourishment of the departed and perform all the rites of the year; thus the departed attains liberation.
A brahmin's property enjoyed even out of affection burns the family for seven generations; the same taken by theft burns it as long as the moon and stars endure.
A man might sometimes digest iron filings and powdered stone, but what man in the three worlds can digest a brahmin's property?
Through destroying the property of the gods, seizing a brahmin's property, and transgressing against brahmins, families fall into ruin.
There is no transgression against a brahmin devoid of learning; one does not leave a blazing fire and pour oblations into ashes.
Gifts and offerings to gods and ancestors made at a sankranti the sun returns again and again until the end of seven kalpas.

Among receiving gifts, teaching and officiating at sacrifices, they call receiving gifts the most desirable; one is purified from receiving by japa and oblation, but the Vedas do not purify the act of officiating.
One who is always doing japa and oblations and avoids food cooked by others is not stained even if he accepts the whole earth full of jewels.
If someone dies through negligence, by water or the like, the chief of his household should perform all the rites for him according to rule.
A mortal should not, through negligence or at will, go before a serpent; on the fifth lunar day of both fortnights one should worship the Naga.
One should draw with flour on the ground the figure of the Nagas and worship it with white flowers, fragrant substances and sandal paste,
offer incense and a lamp, scatter white rice grains, and offer raw flour, cooked food and milk.
Standing before it, one should speak thus while offering coins and garments; on that day one should eat sweet food and complete the shraddha to the gods.
Then one should give a golden Naga, according to one's means, to an excellent brahmin, and, giving a cow, say, 'May the king of Nagas be pleased.'

One should perform the other rites as before, according to one's means, following the rule of one's own Vedic branch, and so do everything properly; thus one frees them from the state of ghosts and leads them on the path to heaven.
Even without being away from home, if the two (dates) have been forgotten, they should still be observed as before on the anniversary of death.
If someone in the house dies while the householder is away, and after the impurity has passed the shraddha rite has been begun,
and the householder returns and learns what has happened there, then the impurity applies to the householder and those persons, but not to the materials.
If the shraddha has been begun in full by the son or another, it should be completed there, and the householder should keep at a distance.
If neither giver nor eater knew of the impurity of birth or death, no fault is ever attributed to either of them.
But if one of them knew of the impurity of birth or death, the fault falls only on the eater; the giver is not defiled.
One who observes the day of death in the manner described always delivers even one whose day of death is unknown.
In the daily shraddha, having devoutly worshipped the brahmins with perfumes and the like, one should properly dedicate it to all the hosts of ancestors together.
Invocation, the cry of svadha, the rice-balls, the offering into fire and the like, the rules of celibacy and so on, and the Vishvedevas —
these should be left out in the daily shraddha; one should prepare food to be eaten, give a fee according to one's means, and dismiss them with salutations.
The feeding of brahmins that one gives in honour of the gods, the Vishvedevas and others, should be done like the daily shraddha; it is called the shraddha to the gods.
The shraddha to the mothers should be done first, and the ancestral one at the beginning of the rite; and on the following day, at an occasion of prosperity, to the maternal grandfathers.
One should perform the three shraddhas, and the Vaishvadeva in the tantric manner.
One should offer first to the mothers, then to the fathers, and likewise to the maternal grandfathers — in this order.
In the shraddha to the mothers, if brahmins are lacking, one should honour eight virtuous women of good family who have husbands and sons.
For works of sacrifice and public merit one should perform the abhyudaya shraddha, and on occasions such as portents, like the daily shraddha.

The daily, the divine, the prosperity, the desire-motivated and the occasional shraddhas — performing them in the manner described one gains success. This I have told you, Tarkshya; what else do you ask?
One who eats at the eleventh-day rite of a dead man is reborn [as such]; one who promises wealth to brahmins but does not give it becomes a jackal.
One who goes against the king becomes a tusked beast; a thief becomes a dung-eating boar; a seller of fruit becomes a sariva; the husband of a shudra woman becomes a bull.
One who touches fire with his foot becomes a cat; one who eats others' flesh becomes diseased; one who goes to a menstruating woman becomes a eunuch; one who steals perfumes becomes foul-smelling.
Whoever steals another's property, whatever it is, little or much, is born among animals; there is no doubt.
These and other signs, O lord of birds, arising from their own deeds, are seen in men.
So one who has done evil, having experienced the hells in turn, is born, through the remainder of his karma, in the wombs described.
Then for a hundred births among mortals and all creatures, O Kashyapa, he is born, without doubt, until good and bad are balanced.
When through the union of woman and man the semen and blood are held together, he is born composed of the five elements, endowed with them.
Senses, mind, vital breaths, knowledge, lifespan, happiness, steadfastness, retention, impulse, sorrow and false ego,
effort, form and colour, attachment and aversion, existence and non-existence — all this belongs to that self, beginningless, which seeks a beginning.
Then, for one bound by his own karma, the embryo grows, as I described to you earlier the marks of a creature.
Thus the wheel turns in the fourfold host of beings; the arising and perishing of embodied beings takes place, Tarkshya.
By one's own dharma one rises, and by adharma one goes down; this happens to all classes through straying from their own dharma, O bird.
The acts of giving, enjoyment and the like seen in the state of gods and men, O Vainateya — all that is fruit born of karma.
In the terrible, evil hell earned through forbidden action, desire and anger, he falls again, and there is no rescue for him.
If ever, by good fortune, the wish to cross over should arise, hear, Kashyapa, how it may become favourable.
At the solstice, the equinox, the holy vyatipata, at daybreak, at an eclipse of moon or sun, at a sankranti or on the new-moon day,
and at other holy times, an excellent gift is given; or whenever there is faith, one should surely give.
That itself is the time for giving, since prosperity is unstable; bodies are impermanent and wealth is not everlasting.
Death is always near; one should gather dharma. One should prepare an auspicious Vaitarani cow, black or reddish,
with golden horns and silver hooves, with a bronze milking vessel, covered with a pair of black cloths and furnished with the seven grains.
On a heap of a drona of cotton, in a copper vessel, one should make a golden Yama holding an iron staff. Binding a raft of sugarcane stalks with strong ties,
placing on the raft the cow born of the Sun's body, one should present it to a brahmin, with an umbrella and sandals,
and offer the brahmin a ring and garments. Holding kusha grass with water, one should utter this mantra:

Having heard of the river Vaitarani at the most dreadful gate of Yama, and wishing to cross it, I give you this Vaitarani; salutations.
garudpurana:286:31	May cows be before me, may cows be at my sides, may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
garudpurana:286:32	O best of brahmins, form of Vishnu, god on earth, lift me up; this Vaitarani with its fee is given by me to you; salutations.
Having circumambulated Dharmaraja, the Lord of all, and the cow called Vaitarani, one should present all to the brahmin.
Holding the cow's tail and placing the brahmin in front, one should say: "O cow, wait for me at Yama's most fearful gate,
to carry me across, O queen of gods; salutations to you, Vaitarani." One should follow the brahmin as he goes and bring everything to his house.
When this is done, O Vainateya, that river becomes easy to cross. The man on earth who gives this obtains all his desires,
and through the power of this good deed, happiness here and hereafter. A gift made while in health is multiplied a thousandfold, while ill a hundredfold;
and a gift made for one already dead, in his absence, is held to be only equal. So one should give with one's own hand; after death, who will give for whom?
Of those without the dharma of giving, living miserly and unseen — with this unstable body one should perform lasting deeds.
For the breaths will surely depart, like guests.
This I have told you, king of birds: the whole drama of the host of creatures. For the release of the departed and for the good and welfare of the world, one should perform the rites after death.
Suta said: Thus instructed, O brahmins, by the mighty Vishnu, Garuda, having heard of the conduct of the departed, was satisfied.
He asked Keshava again about vows, tirthas and all else, meditating in his mind on the Lord of all, the cause of all causes.
O sages, all this concerning the origin of creatures, death and birth, the state of the departed and the rites after death,
I have told completely as a basis for liberation. Theirs is gain, theirs is victory — how could they be defeated, in whose hearts dwells Janardana, dark as the blue lotus?
Dharma triumphs, not adharma; truth triumphs, not falsehood; forbearance triumphs, not anger; Vishnu triumphs, not the asuras.
Vishnu is mother, Vishnu is father, Vishnu is one's own people and kin; for those whose understanding is steady thus, there is no bad fate.
Auspicious is the blessed Vishnu, auspicious the one whose banner bears Garuda, auspicious the lotus-eyed one; Hari is the abode of auspiciousness.
Hari, the Bhagirathi and brahmins; brahmins, the Bhagirathi and Hari; the Bhagirathi, Hari and brahmins — this is the essence in the three worlds.
Having drunk this Vaishnava nectar of words from Suta's lips, adorned with the meaning of all scriptures, the sages were satisfied.
They praised one another and Suta, the seer of all aims, and the sages led by Shaunaka attained incomparable joy.
Whether impure or pure, or in whatever state, whoever remembers the lotus-eyed one is pure within and without.

Your treasury is burnt by fire, your hoard of wealth and grain taken by your sons; only the good words and store of dharma you have made go with you, following behind.
garudpurana:287:36	No one who has died is seen to come back, whether king, ascetic or best of brahmins; the rash mortal who has died perishes, even he who stands on the earth.
So speak those attendants, with the Kinnaras; and he, full of despair, taking courage and hearing the wondrous words of the attendants, speaks, O king of birds, having become human:

Through the power of giving one sits in a celestial car; dharma is the father, compassion the mother, sweet and meaningful speech the wife, bathing at a holy tirtha and a good circle of kin —
garudpurana:287:39	all the good deeds placed in one's hand — then heaven becomes like your servant. The righteous will attain great happiness, and the sinner every kind of sorrow.

The man who is righteous, has conquered pride and anger, is humble through learning, does not torment others, is content with his own wife and keeps far from others' wives — such a man is worthy of reverence on earth.

The giver of sweet food, the performer of the agnihotra, the knower of Vedanta, one who lives to see a thousand moons, one who fasts for a month, and a faithful wife — these six in the world of the living are to be revered by me.
A man of such conduct who builds a step-well with a well, a tank with water, a fine water-shed, a house or a temple of the gods — that man is best in dharma.
A year's food given to a knower of the Veda, the marriage of a maiden, freeing a brahmin from debt, well-ploughed land given to relieve distress — all this is good deed.
Whoever hears or sings with a pure heart this chapter, the essence of good deeds, is of noble family and endowed with dharma, and surely goes to the supreme abode of the universe.
Where hypocrites devoid of knowledge and detachment do not go — the wise go to that goal; I will tell you of them.

Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever devoted to the Self, their desires turned away, freed from the pairs called pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable state.
Whoever bathes in the tirtha of the mind, whose lake is knowledge and whose water is truth, which removes the dirt of attachment and aversion, surely attains liberation.
Whoever, resorting to mature detachment, worships me with undivided devotion, with complete vision and serene self, surely attains liberation.
Whoever leaves his home and dwells at a tirtha, awaiting death, and dies in the fields of liberation, surely attains liberation.
Ayodhya, Mathura, Maya, Kashi, Kanchi, Avantika and the city of Dvaravati — know these seven as givers of liberation.
Thus I have told you, Tarkshya, the eternal dharma of liberation; hearing it, together with knowledge and detachment, one attains liberation.
The knowers of truth go to liberation, righteous men to heaven, sinners to a bad fate; birds and others wander in the cycle of birth.
Suta said: Having thus heard from the Lord's mouth the conclusive answers to his questions, Tarkshya, his body thrilling with joy, bowed to the Lord of the world.
My great doubt has been destroyed by the light of your words. Having said this and taken leave of Vishnu, he went to Kashyapa's hermitage.
One goes at once to another body, or goes after a delay; between these two, likewise, there is no contradiction for you.
He told everything, dear one, just as he had heard it from the Lord; and Marichi's son too rejoiced on hearing the words of Lakshmi's lord.
Your doubt, O brahmins, has been removed by me; I have told the most wondrous Purana named after Suparna.
Tarkshya obtained it from Hari, and Bhrigu from Tarkshya; Vasishtha received it from Bhrigu, and then Vamadeva;
the sage Parashara obtained it, from him Vyasa, and from him I; and I have told you this supreme secret of Hari.
The mortal who hears this or recites it obtains happiness everywhere, in this world and the next.
The sorrow described here of one going to Samyamani — through the merit of hearing this, one is freed from it.
Since hearing here of the ripening of karma and the like brings detachment to men, therefore it should indeed be heard.

With senses conquered, worship this Krishna, lord of sages, from whom arose speech that is a stream of the essence of nectar; drinking even a drop of it, its syllables and forms, with the cup of the ears, one attains oneness with the Self.
Vyasa said: Having drunk this Vaishnava nectar of words from Suta's lips, adorned with the meaning of all scriptures, the sages were satisfied.
They praised one another and Suta, the seer of all aims, and the sages led by Shaunaka attained incomparable joy.
Having heard through Suta's voice these words of Hari which dispelled the doubts of the lord of birds, the sage Shaunaka too took them deeply to heart.
Then the sages honoured Suta again and again with noble words, declaring, "Blessed are you here, Suta," and, when the sacrifice was over, dismissed him.
The Garuda Purana is holy, purifying and destroys sin; it fulfils the wishes of those who hear it, and should always be heard.
Having heard it, one should give all the gifts to the reciter — the bed and the rest described earlier; otherwise it will not bear fruit.
One should first worship the Purana and then the reciter, respectfully, with clothes, ornaments, gifts of cows and fees.
With gifts of food, gold and land in abundance one should devotedly honour the reciter to obtain great fruit of merit.
The mortal who hears this, or recites it as it is, escapes the terrible torments and, his sins shaken off, goes to heaven.
Having praised thus, Rudra fell silent, O best of brahmins. Then the goddess Varuni, born after Shesha, spoke these words.
Varuni said: "O lord of Lakshmi, lord of Brahma, lord of Manu, lord of speech, lord of Rudra, lord of men — I am not able to praise your qualities, nor is Parvati, nor the wife of Suparna.
I am ten times lower than Shesha; protect me always, O Lord of the worlds."
Having praised thus, Varuni fell silent, O lord of birds. Then Sauparni, born after her, of Brahma's line, began.

Sauparni said: "O Hari, Lord of the world, I have no power to praise your qualities with speech, nor, O Hari, to hear your story with the ears. Who on earth truly knows that meaning of the word Bhagavan, the one who remembers your true form, O God?
So I have no power to praise your qualities, O lord of birds' lord; I am always ten times lower."
Having praised thus, Sauparni fell silent, O lord of birds. Then Girija, born after Rudra, began to praise.
Parvati said: "Govinda, Narayana, Vasudeva — I have no purpose at all to gain from you, O master, other than your name; by speech you are always the one form of good fortune.
Your single name 'Narayana' is supremely able to grant the riches of detachment and devotion, to destroy countless slayings of Brahma and the like, and crores of sins of violating the teacher's wife.
I am entitled only to your name, O great Lord, not to your qualities; I have no power to praise; I am ten times lower than Rudra,
and ever lower — there is no need to consider this." Having praised thus, Girija fell silent, O lord of birds.
Now I will tell of those born after them; hear them, O lord of birds. Born after the wife of Pravaha, Vishvaksena the attendant, the fortunate son of Vayu, began to praise Hari.
Vishvaksena said: "The Lord Krishna, giver of liberation, full bliss — if there is always supreme devotion, which is the means to direct realization,
and likewise sincere devotion toward the good, from one's own teacher up to Brahma, according to their worthiness,
and if there is love, O egg-born one, for beings such as the tulasi, and remembrance, then surely there will be destruction [of bondage]; there is no doubt."
Having praised thus, the fortunate Vishvaksena, O great lord, fell silent, O Garuda, with joined palms and neck bowed: "I am lower than Mitra; there is no need to consider this."
Kavasha, Harita, Kanva, Virupa and Musala, Vishnuvriddha, Atreya, Shrivatsa and Vatsala,
Bhargava, Apnavana, Mandukeya, Manduka, Jabali and Vitihavya,
Gritsamada and Shaunaka — such are the sages remembered. By merely hearing of them Hari is always pleased.

I speak of sixteen thousand; hear, Tarkshya, of my wives. The sixteen thousand wives of mine who are sons of Agni are equal to the Ajana gods; there is no need to consider this.
garudpurana:297:17	Tvashtr's daughter Kasheru is superior in qualities among them. Now I will tell of those born after them; listen well, O lord of birds.
garudpurana:297:18	The ancestors other than the seven are a hundred times lower than the Ajana gods, and the ancestors are likewise higher — this is the view of the knowers of the Veda.
garudpurana:297:19	Now I will tell of those born after them; hear, best of brahmins: the divine Gandharvas, apart from the eight and the hundred and eight,
garudpurana:297:20	are chiefly the servants of the gods, a hundred times lower in bliss than those; the hosts are always to be commanded by the gods with their own mouths.
garudpurana:297:21	The divine Gandharvas have been described; those below them are a hundred times lower; below them are known the kings of the earth, lower by a hundredfold.
garudpurana:297:22	Below them, a hundredfold lower, are known the best groups among men. Having spoken of these incidental matters, I return to the subject. So Brahma and the other gods, and Lakshmi and the others in every way,
garudpurana:297:23	having praised, all stood silent with joined palms, O brahmin.
garudpurana:297:24	Thus praised, the Lord of gods, the imperishable Blessed Hari, considered in his mind how to give them their abodes.
garudpurana:297:25	This is purifying, health-giving, meritorious and destroys sin; it brings about Hari's grace and is the means to the bliss of one's true nature.
garudpurana:297:26	Those men here, O brahmins, who do not read this hymn or hear it daily are all deceivers.
garudpurana:297:27	The vilest of men who eat without always remembering the Inner One eat nothing but filth teeming with hundreds of worms.
garudpurana:298:32	In a hundred births he attains the position of Brahma, and afterwards Hari's abode. From the fortieth kalpa of Brahma, O lord of birds,
garudpurana:298:33	there comes direct realization for Rudra too, and the exhaustion of his prarabdha karma. In the forty-first kalpa he attains the position of Shesha, O you of good vows,
garudpurana:298:34	and goes to liberation together with Brahma, rightly and not otherwise. From the twentieth kalpa of Brahma, the Supreme One,
garudpurana:298:35	there comes direct realization for Indra too, and the exhaustion of his prarabdha; together with Brahma he goes to Hari, the supreme Narayana.
garudpurana:298:36	Garuda said: From the eighty-fifth kalpa of Brahma, O great Lord, there comes direct realization for Rudra too, and the exhaustion of his prarabdha —
so I heard, O Brahman, as told by Brahma, dear to Hari; yet you have said otherwise, O Shri Krishna, and a doubt troubles me.
So cut away my doubt, so that it does not arise again." Hearing his words, Krishna spoke:
Shri Krishna said: "There is no contradiction at all between what Brahma said and what I have said; doubt belongs to those of ignorant vision, never to the wise.
Eighty is declared as eight tens and five eights, O lord of birds; so the four-faced one spoke of forty kalpas of Brahma.
Because the principles are so very secret, Brahma spoke thus long ago; but the intended meaning is to be understood just so; there is no doubt.
Those who understand it as eighty-five kalpas of Brahma, O brahmin, enter blind darkness; truly, truly, I declare it.
Beyond the Viraja, O brahmin, is the unmanifested sky, endless and boundless; Lakshmi is its presiding deity.
It has no measure by number, O great lord, nor is it described by class, ever; there is no doubt.
Brahma, presiding over the cosmic egg, then became the one called Viraj; having constructed it so, the imperishable Lord Hari,
especially together with the gods who preside over the principles, O Garuda, pervading it below and above, Hari abides always.
Such is the account of the primary creation; now hear the secondary, O king of birds."
Garuda said: "The creation you described earlier I have heard well, O Hari.
What is to be known as primary (prakrita), and what as secondary (vaikrita), O Lord? Explain this to me at length, for I am eager to hear."
Shri Krishna said: "Those beginning with the unmanifest and ending with earth, arising outside the cosmic egg — all these are called primary; by knowing them one is liberated.
The cosmic egg is to be known as secondary; the creation within the cosmic egg, O lord of birds, which the good speak of, is called secondary.
Creation and dissolution, worldly existence and devotion, the gods and chief sages, and the worlds beginning with Bhu
are of beginningless and endless time, always of one kind; this flow of the world is real, never false in any way.
Those who say otherwise are destroyers of all; this flow of the world is real, and so is service to Hari.
Truly, truly, again truly, with raised arm it is declared: there is no scripture higher than the Veda, and no god higher than Keshava.
For those who abandon Keshava, highest of all, and worship another, blind darkness is to be known, for their ancestors and teachers too.
Now hear, lord of birds, the excellent secondary creation; whoever in the world understands it rightly goes to the supreme abode."
When the cause exists, then the effect exists, O Lord; if you answer with that intended meaning,
then tell me, O fortunate one, how can there be fear and the like for him? Let there be fear and the like — what harm would that be to us?"
Addressed thus, Govinda gave the reason for that too: "Fear would be an effect of ignorance, and here there is no effect without a cause.
He is pleased thinking of Brahman; so sleep is there. If ignorance and the like were in Brahma, it could in no way be his.
How is he seen to be happy? He will not act in any way." "And how, tell me, does knowledge become manifest until liberation?
If his ignorance is not real, O great Lord, how, tell me, O Brahman, does he listen with such great eagerness?"
Hearing his words, Krishna said: "Know that his fear is not real, O wise one.
His fear of me is seen only for the pleasure of Hari; his appearing fearful and desirous is declared unreal.
For one who has reached the last trace of prarabdha, O lord of birds, there is no sorrow or ignorance at all; how could it be in him?
Following Vishnu's command, he imitates fear, and by that Hari is pleased with him; there is no doubt of this.
Brahma always listens, yet one should not think him ignorant because of that; sometimes Brahma is seen to be sorrowful, yet he is not, O lord of birds.
If Brahma seems not to know, it is only for the pleasure of Hari; Brahma is seen as if sorrowful to delude the ignorant.
As far as knowledge remains without exceeding worthiness, so far it exists for Brahma; there is no need to consider this.
The manifestation of knowledge means the reverent attention to knowledge already present; attaining knowledge is what is called the manifestation of knowledge.
So there is no ignorance and the like in Brahma, the Supreme One. The four-faced Brahma was born from the golden lotus;
always endowed with reflection, he performed self-reflection to delude the ignorant and only for the pleasure of Hari.
His resolve too was likewise, not made through ignorance. Reflecting, 'Who created me here?', that lord,
Brahma, entered the stalk of the lotus to investigate it."
Thinking of father, mother and brahmins as forms of Hari; thinking of the dependent Rudra as one with Hari and the like;
thinking of Vishnu as not different from the sun and so on; thinking 'The sun alone is highest of all, and Vishnu and the rest are its servants' —
such thinking is a fault and is called reviling Hari. Those who bow to lingas that are not self-manifest, and to ashvattha trees and tulasi plants,
while neglecting the shalagrama — all of them are guilty of reviling Hari.
Those who are fit for liberation, if out of ignorance they make the Supreme Lord separate in these, O Lord,
then they surely come to sorrow in time; so all those who always make him separate in these
are to be known as unwise; there is no need to consider this. Those who bow to lingas that are not self-manifest
are all to be known as asuras, and not otherwise in any way. Those who bow to an empty ashvattha,
to a tulasi less than two months old, or to a new cow that has not calved, are all to be known as asuras; there is no need to consider this.
Those from shrubs to men are to be known as the arms of Brahma. Up to our lifespan of a hundred years, one Kali is remembered.
In Kali there is the measure of a kalpa, and at the end of Kali too; on that day, in the form of Brahma, they go near to darkness.
Staying there, they await the path of the world, without doubt, harassed by the servants of Vayu who accomplish the works of Vishnu.
After a hundred years, for all of them together with Kali, the subtle body will be broken by the blow of Vayu's mace.
They enter blind darkness in every way, according to their gradation; even in the blind darkness of worldly existence — there is no need to consider this.
Kali alone is the lowest at the end of all, without doubt; there is never anyone equal to him as a reviler of Vishnu's devotees.
In worldly existence and in blind darkness he everywhere reviles Hari; he takes false giving for knowledge and sorrow for happiness.
Therefore nowhere in the world is there a devotee of Shiva equal to Kali; he is declared to be Duryodhana, whose very nature is endless sorrow.
